title: भारतसँग जलस्रोत सहकार्यलाई प्राथमिकता दिन पूर्वकूटनीतिज्ञको सुझाव

During the visit, discussions are expected to be held on the utilization of water resources and energy cooperation, including the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project. To make water resources cooperation between Nepal and India effective, the challenge is to implement past agreements and resolve differences in benefit sharing. काठमाडौं । प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहको आसन्न भारत भ्रमणमा नेपालको जलस्रोतलाई दुई देशको साझा समृद्धिको आधार बनाउने प्रस्ताव अघि सार्न पूर्वकूटनीतिज्ञहरूले सुझाव दिएका छन् । उनीहरूले जलविद्युत् उत्पादन र व्यापारसँगै सिँचाइ, खानेपानी तथा बाढी नियन्त्रणमा सहकार्य विस्तार गरेर दुवै देशले लाभ लिन सक्ने बताएका हुन् । प्रधानमन्त्री शाह यही मंसिर ६ र ७ गते दुईदिने भारत भ्रमणमा जाँदै छन् । भ्रमणका क्रममा नेपाल–भारतबीच जलस्रोतको उपयोग, ऊर्जा सहकार्य र पञ्चेश्वर बहुउद्देश्यीय आयोजनासहितका विषयमा छलफल हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ । लामो समयदेखि चर्चामा रहे पनि कार्यान्वयनमा अघि बढ्न नसकेको पञ्चेश्वर आयोजनालाई पनि भ्रमणको महत्वपूर्ण एजेन्डा बनाउनुपर्ने उनीहरूको सुझाव छ । भारतका लागि नेपालका पूर्वराजदूत दीपकुमार उपाध्यायले नेपालको पानीलाई समस्याका रूपमा नभई दुवै देशका लागि वरदान बनाउनुपर्ने बताए । जलस्रोतको बहुउपयोगबाट नेपाल र भारत दुवैले आर्थिक तथा सामाजिक लाभ लिन सक्ने भएकाले त्यसका लागि साझा सहकार्य आवश्यक रहेको उनको भनाइ छ । ‘नेपालको पानीलाई समस्याका रूपमा होइन, दुवै देशका लागि वरदान बनाउन सकिन्छ,’ उपाध्यायले भने । उनका अनुसार नेपालको जलस्रोतबाट विद्युत् उत्पादन र व्यापार मात्रै नभई सिँचाइ, खानेपानी तथा बाढी नियन्त्रणमा समेत लाभ लिन सकिन्छ । नेपालमा प्रत्येक वर्ष बाढी र डुबानका कारण ठूलो जनधनको क्षति हुने गरेको छ । यसले नेपालको कृषि, जनजीवन र पूर्वाधारमा असर पार्नुका साथै भारतका सीमावर्ती क्षेत्रमा पनि समस्या सिर्जना गर्ने गरेको छ । त्यसैले नदी व्यवस्थापन, बाढी नियन्त्रण र जलस्रोतको उपयोगलाई छुट्टाछुट्टै विषयका रूपमा नभई समग्र क्षेत्रीय सहकार्यका रूपमा अघि बढाउनुपर्ने उपाध्यायको सुझाव छ । अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कानुन र मान्यताअनुसार तेस्रो पक्षको हितसमेत ध्यानमा राखेर जलस्रोतको बहुउपयोग गर्न भारत सकारात्मक हुनुपर्ने उनले बताए । उपाध्यायले जलस्रोतसम्बन्धी सहकार्यलाई नेपालको आर्थिक विकास र भारतको आवश्यकतासँग जोडेर अघि बढाउनुपर्ने बताए । यसका लागि विगतमा भएका सहमति कार्यान्वयन गर्दै नयाँ सहकार्यका आधार खोज्नुपर्ने उनको धारणा छ । पञ्चेश्वर बहुउद्देश्यीय आयोजनालाई पनि उनले नेपाल–भारत जलस्रोत सहकार्यको महत्वपूर्ण उदाहरणका रूपमा अघि बढाउन सकिने बताए । दुई देशबीचको सहमतिअनुसार अघि बढ्नुपर्ने यस्ता आयोजनामा आपसी समझदारी र लाभको बाँडफाँट स्पष्ट हुनुपर्ने उनको भनाइ छ । डेनमार्कका लागि नेपालका राजदूत विजयकान्त कर्णले पनि प्रधानमन्त्रीको भारत भ्रमणमा ऊर्जा सहकार्य र पञ्चेश्वर आयोजनाको विषय उठ्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको बताए । उनका अनुसार भ्रमणमा विपद् व्यवस्थापन, पूर्वाधार विकास, हवाई रुट, ऊर्जा सहकार्य र पञ्चेश्वर बहुउद्देश्यीय आयोजनालगायत विषयमा छलफल हुन सक्छ । कर्णले नेपालमा हालै आएको बाढीबाट भएको क्षतिको पुनर्निर्माण तथा व्यवस्थापनमा भारतको सहयोग आवश्यक रहेको बताए । यसका लागि नेपालले भारतसँग करिब दुई अर्ब अमेरिकी डलर बराबरको सहयोग क्रेडिट लाइन तथा अनुदानका रूपमा उपलब्ध गराउन प्रस्ताव गरेको उनले जानकारी दिए । बाढी नियन्त्रण र विपद् व्यवस्थापनमा दुई देशबीच सहकार्य बढाउनु आवश्यक रहेको उनको भनाइ छ । नदी तथा जलाधार क्षेत्रको व्यवस्थापनमा समन्वय हुन सके नेपाल र भारत दुवैतर्फ हुने क्षति न्यूनीकरण गर्न सकिने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ । यसैबीच, चीनका लागि नेपालका पूर्वराजदूत लीलामणि पौडेलले प्रधानमन्त्रीले भारतसँगको छलफलमा नेपालको राष्ट्रिय हितलाई प्राथमिकतामा राख्नुपर्ने बताए । उनले असंलग्न परराष्ट्र नीतिको सिद्धान्तभित्र रहेर स्वतन्त्र र सार्वभौम मुलुकका रूपमा राष्ट्रिय हित प्रवर्द्धन गर्नुपर्ने धारणा राखे । नेपाल र भारतबीच जलस्रोतलगायतका विषयमा विगतमा भएका सन्धि, सम्झौता र समझदारीलाई प्रभावकारी रूपमा कार्यान्वयन गर्नुपर्ने उनको भनाइ छ । बलियो जनसमर्थनसहित निर्वाचित सरकारले राष्ट्रिय हितका विषय स्पष्ट रूपमा उठाउन सक्ने अवसर रहेको उनले बताए । नेपाल र भारतबीच जलस्रोत उपयोगका विषयमा लामो समयदेखि विभिन्न द्विपक्षीय संयन्त्रमार्फत छलफल हुँदै आएको छ । तर, पञ्चेश्वरजस्ता महत्वपूर्ण आयोजना अघि बढाउन पानीको उपयोग र लाभ बाँडफाँटमा रहेका मतभेद समाधान गर्नुपर्ने चुनौती कायमै छ । यस्तो अवस्थामा प्रधानमन्त्रीको भ्रमणलाई जलस्रोत सहकार्यमा ठोस प्रगति खोज्ने अवसरका रूपमा उपयोग गर्नुपर्ने पूर्वकूटनीतिज्ञहरूको सुझाव छ । पार्वती भण्डारी, नेपाल न्यूज बैंक Kathmandu. Former diplomats have suggested that Prime Minister Balendra Shah's upcoming visit to India should bring forward a proposal to make Nepal's water resources a basis for shared prosperity for the two countries. They said that both countries could benefit from expanding cooperation in irrigation, drinking water and flood control, along with hydropower generation and trade. Prime Minister Shah is leaving for a two-day visit to India on November 20 and 21. During the visit, issues including water resource utilization, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project between Nepal and India are expected to be discussed. They suggest that the Pancheshwar Project, which has been in the news for a long time but has not been implemented, should also be made an important agenda of the visit. Former Nepali Ambassador to India Deep Kumar Upadhyay said that Nepal's water should not be seen as a problem but a boon for both countries. He said that joint cooperation is necessary as both Nepal and India can reap economic and social benefits from the multiple use of water resources. "Nepal's water can be made a blessing for both countries, not a problem," Upadhyay said. According to him, Nepal's water resources can be used not only for electricity generation and trade, but also for irrigation, drinking water and flood control. Every year, floods and inundations cause huge losses of life and property in Nepal. This affects Nepal's agriculture, livelihoods and infrastructure, and also creates problems in the border areas of India. Therefore, Upadhyay suggests that river management, flood control and water resource utilization should be taken forward as a comprehensive regional cooperation rather than as separate issues. He said that India should be positive in multi-utilization of water resources, keeping in mind the interests of third parties as per international law and norms. Upadhyaya said that cooperation on water resources should be taken forward by linking it to Nepal's economic development and India's needs. For this, he believes that new bases for cooperation should be found by implementing past agreements. He also said that the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project can be taken forward as an important example of Nepal-India water resources cooperation. He said that such projects should be carried out as per the agreement between the two countries, with clear mutual understanding and benefit sharing. Nepal's Ambassador to Denmark, Vijayakanta Karna, also said that the issue of energy cooperation and the Pancheshwar project is expected to be raised during the Prime Minister's visit to India. According to him, the visit may include discussions on disaster management, infrastructure development, air routes, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar multipurpose project. Karna said that India's assistance is needed in the reconstruction and management of the damage caused by the recent floods in Nepal. For this, Nepal has proposed to provide India with assistance worth about two billion US dollars in the form of a credit line and grant, he informed. He said that there is a need to increase cooperation between the two countries in flood control and disaster management. It is expected that if there is coordination in the management of rivers and watersheds, the damage to both Nepal and India can be minimized. Meanwhile, former Nepali Ambassador to China Leelamani Poudel said that the Prime Minister should prioritize Nepal's national interests in his discussions with India. He opined that Nepal should promote its national interests as an independent and sovereign country within the principle of non-aligned foreign policy. He said that the treaties, agreements and understandings reached between Nepal and India on issues including water resources should be effectively implemented. He said that there is an opportunity for an elected government with strong public support to clearly raise issues of national interest. Discussions on water resource utilization between Nepal and India have been ongoing for a long time through various bilateral mechanisms. However, the challenge of resolving differences over water use and benefit sharing remains to move forward with important projects like Pancheshwar. In such a situation, former diplomats suggest that the Prime Minister's visit should be used as an opportunity to seek concrete progress in water resources cooperation. Parvati Bhandari, Nepal News Bank

व्यवस्थापनमा भारतको सहयोग आवश्यक रहेको बताए । यसका लागि नेपालले भारतसँग करिब दुई अर्ब अमेरिकी डलर बराबरको सहयोग क्रेडिट लाइन तथा अनुदानका रूपमा उपलब्ध गराउन प्रस्ताव गरेको उनले जानकारी दिए । बाढी Former diplomats have suggested that Prime Minister Balendra Shah's upcoming visit to India should bring forward a proposal to make Nepal's water resources a basis for shared prosperity for the two countries. They said that both countries could benefit from expanding cooperation in irrigation, drinking water and flood control, along with hydropower generation and trade. Prime Minister Shah is leaving for a two-day visit to India on November 20 and 21. During the visit, issues including water resource utilization, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project between Nepal and India are expected to be discussed. They suggest that the Pancheshwar Project, which has been in the news for a long time but has not been implemented, should also be made an important agenda of the visit. Former Nepali Ambassador to India Deep Kumar Upadhyay said that Nepal's water should not be seen as a problem but a boon for both countries. He said that joint cooperation is necessary as both Nepal and India can reap economic and social benefits from the multiple use of water resources. "Nepal's water can be made a blessing for both countries, not a problem," Upadhyay said. According to him, Nepal's water resources can be used not only for electricity generation and trade, but also for irrigation, drinking water and flood control. Every year, floods and inundations cause huge losses of life and property in Nepal. This affects Nepal's agriculture, livelihoods and infrastructure, and also creates problems in the border areas of India. Therefore, Upadhyay suggests that river management, flood control and water resource utilization should be taken forward as a comprehensive regional cooperation rather than as separate issues. He said that India should be positive in multi-utilization of water resources, keeping in mind the interests of third parties as per international law and norms. Upadhyaya said that cooperation on water resources should be taken forward by linking it to Nepal's economic development and India's needs. For this, he believes that new bases for cooperation should be found by implementing past agreements. He also said that the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project can be taken forward as an important example of Nepal-India water resources cooperation. He said that such projects should be carried out as per the agreement between the two countries, with clear mutual understanding and benefit sharing. Nepal's Ambassador to Denmark, Vijayakanta Karna, also said that the issue of energy cooperation and the Pancheshwar project is expected to be raised during the Prime Minister's visit to India. According to him, the visit may include discussions on disaster management, infrastructure development, air routes, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar multipurpose project. Karna said that India's assistance is needed in the reconstruction and management of the damage caused by the recent floods in Nepal. For this, Nepal has proposed to provide India with assistance worth about two billion US dollars in the form of a credit line and grant, he informed. He said that there is a need to increase cooperation between the two countries in flood control and disaster management. It is expected that if there is coordination in the management of rivers and watersheds, the damage to both Nepal and India can be minimized. Meanwhile, former Nepali Ambassador to China Leelamani Poudel said that the Prime Minister should prioritize Nepal's national interests in his discussions with India. He opined that Nepal should promote its national interests as an independent and sovereign country within the principle of non-aligned foreign policy. He said that the treaties, agreements and understandings reached between Nepal and India on issues including water resources should be effectively implemented. He said that there is an opportunity for an elected government with strong public support to clearly raise issues of national interest. Discussions on water resource utilization between Nepal and India have been ongoing for a long time through various bilateral mechanisms. However, the challenge of resolving differences over water use and benefit sharing remains to move forward with important projects like Pancheshwar. In such a situation, former diplomats suggest that the Prime Minister's visit should be used as an opportunity to seek concrete progress in water resources cooperation. Former diplomats have suggested that Prime Minister Balendra Shah's upcoming visit to India should bring forward a proposal to make Nepal's water resources a basis for shared prosperity for the two countries. They said that both countries could benefit from expanding cooperation in irrigation, drinking water and flood control, along with hydropower generation and trade. Prime Minister Shah is leaving for a two-day visit to India on November 20 and 21. During the visit, issues including water resource utilization, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project between Nepal and India are expected to be discussed. They suggest that the Pancheshwar Project, which has been in the news for a long time but has not been implemented, should also be made an important agenda of the visit. Former Nepali Ambassador to India Deep Kumar Upadhyay said that Nepal's water should not be seen as a problem but a boon for both countries. He said that joint cooperation is necessary as both Nepal and India can reap economic and social benefits from the multiple use of water resources. "Nepal's water can be made a blessing for both countries, not a problem," Upadhyay said. According to him, Nepal's water resources can be used not only for electricity generation and trade, but also for irrigation, drinking water and flood control. Every year, floods and inundations cause huge losses of life and property in Nepal. This affects Nepal's agriculture, livelihoods and infrastructure, and also creates problems in the border areas of India. Therefore, Upadhyay suggests that river management, flood control and water resource utilization should be taken forward as a comprehensive regional cooperation rather than as separate issues. He said that India should be positive in multi-utilization of water resources, keeping in mind the interests of third parties as per international law and norms. Upadhyaya said that cooperation on water resources should be taken forward by linking it to Nepal's economic development and India's needs. For this, he believes that new bases for cooperation should be found by implementing past agreements. He also said that the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project can be taken forward as an important example of Nepal-India water resources cooperation. He said that such projects should be carried out as per the agreement between the two countries, with clear mutual understanding and benefit sharing. Nepal's Ambassador to Denmark, Vijayakanta Karna, also said that the issue of energy cooperation and the Pancheshwar project is expected to be raised during the Prime Minister's visit to India. According to him, the visit may include discussions on disaster management, infrastructure development, air routes, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar multipurpose project. Karna said that India's assistance is needed in the reconstruction and management of the damage caused by the recent floods in Nepal. For this, Nepal has proposed to provide India with assistance worth about two billion US dollars in the form of a credit line and grant, he informed. He said that there is a need to increase cooperation between the two countries in flood control and disaster management. It is expected that if there is coordination in the management of rivers and watersheds, the damage to both Nepal and India can be minimized. Meanwhile, former Nepali Ambassador to China Leelamani Poudel said that the Prime Minister should prioritize Nepal's national interests in his discussions with India. He opined that Nepal should promote its national interests as an independent and sovereign country within the principle of non-aligned foreign policy. He said that the treaties, agreements and understandings reached between Nepal and India on issues including water resources should be effectively implemented. He said that there is an opportunity for an elected government with strong public support to clearly raise issues of national interest. Discussions on water resource utilization between Nepal and India have been ongoing for a long time through various bilateral mechanisms. However, the challenge of resolving differences over water use and benefit sharing remains to move forward with important projects like Pancheshwar. In such a situation, former diplomats suggest that the Prime Minister's visit should be used as an opportunity to seek concrete progress in water resources cooperation. Former diplomats have suggested that Prime Minister Balendra Shah's upcoming visit to India should bring forward a proposal to make Nepal's water resources a basis for shared prosperity for the two countries. They said that both countries could benefit from expanding cooperation in irrigation, drinking water and flood control, along with hydropower generation and trade. Prime Minister Shah is leaving for a two-day visit to India on November 20 and 21. During the visit, issues including water resource utilization, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project between Nepal and India are expected to be discussed. They suggest that the Pancheshwar Project, which has been in the news for a long time but has not been implemented, should also be made an important agenda of the visit. Former Nepali Ambassador to India Deep Kumar Upadhyay said that Nepal's water should not be seen as a problem but a boon for both countries. He said that joint cooperation is necessary as both Nepal and India can reap economic and social benefits from the multiple use of water resources. "Nepal's water can be made a blessing for both countries, not a problem," Upadhyay said. According to him, Nepal's water resources can be used not only for electricity generation and trade, but also for irrigation, drinking water and flood control. Every year, floods and inundations cause huge losses of life and property in Nepal. This affects Nepal's agriculture, livelihoods and infrastructure, and also creates problems in the border areas of India. Therefore, Upadhyay suggests that river management, flood control and water resource utilization should be taken forward as a comprehensive regional cooperation rather than as separate issues. He said that India should be positive in multi-utilization of water resources, keeping in mind the interests of third parties as per international law and norms. Upadhyaya said that cooperation on water resources should be taken forward by linking it to Nepal's economic development and India's needs. For this, he believes that new bases for cooperation should be found by implementing past agreements. He also said that the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project can be taken forward as an important example of Nepal-India water resources cooperation. He said that such projects should be carried out as per the agreement between the two countries, with clear mutual understanding and benefit sharing. Nepal's Ambassador to Denmark, Vijayakanta Karna, also said that the issue of energy cooperation and the Pancheshwar project is expected to be raised during the Prime Minister's visit to India. According to him, the visit may include discussions on disaster management, infrastructure development, air routes, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar multipurpose project. Karna said that India's assistance is needed in the reconstruction and management of the damage caused by the recent floods in Nepal. For this, Nepal has proposed to provide India with assistance worth about two billion US dollars in the form of a credit line and grant, he informed. He said that there is a need to increase cooperation between the two countries in flood control and disaster management. It is expected that if there is coordination in the management of rivers and watersheds, the damage to both Nepal and India can be minimized. Meanwhile, former Nepali Ambassador to China Leelamani Poudel said that the Prime Minister should prioritize Nepal's national interests in his discussions with India. He opined that Nepal should promote its national interests as an independent and sovereign country within the principle of non-aligned foreign policy. He said that the treaties, agreements and understandings reached between Nepal and India on issues including water resources should be effectively implemented. He said that there is an opportunity for an elected government with strong public support to clearly raise issues of national interest. Discussions on water resource utilization between Nepal and India have been ongoing for a long time through various bilateral mechanisms. However, the challenge of resolving differences over water use and benefit sharing remains to move forward with important projects like Pancheshwar. In such a situation, former diplomats suggest that the Prime Minister's visit should be used as an opportunity to seek concrete progress in water resources cooperation. उपलब्ध गराउन प्रस्ताव गरेको उनले जानकारी दिए । बाढी नियन्त्रण र विपद् व्यवस्थापनमा दुई देशबीच सहकार्य बढाउनु आवश्यक रहेको उनको भनाइ छ । नदी तथा जलाधार क्षेत्रको व्यवस्थापनमा समन्वय हुन सके नेपाल र भारत दुवैतर्फ हुने क्षति न्यूनीकरण गर्न सकिने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ । यसैबीच, चीनका लागि नेपालका पूर्वराजदूत लीलामणि पौडेलले प्रधानमन्त्रीले भारतसँगको छलफलमा नेपालको राष्ट्रिय हितलाई प्राथमिकतामा Kathmandu. Former diplomats have suggested that Prime Minister Balendra Shah's upcoming visit to India should bring forward a proposal to make Nepal's water resources a basis for shared prosperity for the two countries. They said that both countries could benefit from expanding cooperation in irrigation, drinking water and flood control, along with hydropower generation and trade. Prime Minister Shah is leaving for a two-day visit to India on November 20 and 21. During the visit, issues including water resource utilization, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project between Nepal and India are expected to be discussed. They suggest that the Pancheshwar Project, which has been in the news for a long time but has not been implemented, should also be made an important agenda of the visit. Former Nepali Ambassador to India Deep Kumar Upadhyay said that Nepal's water should not be seen as a problem but a boon for both countries. He said that joint cooperation is necessary as both Nepal and India can reap economic and social benefits from the multiple use of water resources. "Nepal's water can be made a blessing for both countries, not a problem," Upadhyay said. According to him, Nepal's water resources can be used not only for electricity generation and trade, but also for irrigation, drinking water and flood control. Every year, floods and inundations cause huge losses of life and property in Nepal. This affects Nepal's agriculture, livelihoods and infrastructure, and also creates problems in the border areas of India. Therefore, Upadhyay suggests that river management, flood control and water resource utilization should be taken forward as a comprehensive regional cooperation rather than as separate issues. He said that India should be positive in multi-utilization of water resources, keeping in mind the interests of third parties as per international law and norms. Upadhyaya said that cooperation on water resources should be taken forward by linking it to Nepal's economic development and India's needs. For this, he believes that new bases for cooperation should be found by implementing past agreements. He also said that the Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project can be taken forward as an important example of Nepal-India water resources cooperation. He said that such projects should be carried out as per the agreement between the two countries, with clear mutual understanding and benefit sharing. Nepal's Ambassador to Denmark, Vijayakanta Karna, also said that the issue of energy cooperation and the Pancheshwar project is expected to be raised during the Prime Minister's visit to India. According to him, the visit may include discussions on disaster management, infrastructure development, air routes, energy cooperation, and the Pancheshwar multipurpose project. Karna said that India's assistance is needed in the reconstruction and management of the damage caused by the recent floods in Nepal. For this, Nepal has proposed to provide India with assistance worth about two billion US dollars in the form of a credit line and grant, he informed. He said that there is a need to increase cooperation between the two countries in flood control and disaster management. It is expected that if there is coordination in the management of rivers and watersheds, the damage to both Nepal and India can be minimized. Meanwhile, former Nepali Ambassador to China Leelamani Poudel said that the Prime Minister should prioritize Nepal's national interests in his discussions with India. He opined that Nepal should promote its national interests as an independent and sovereign country within the principle of non-aligned foreign policy. He said that the treaties, agreements and understandings reached between Nepal and India on issues including water resources should be effectively implemented. He said that there is an opportunity for an elected government with strong public support to clearly raise issues of national interest. Discussions on water resource utilization between Nepal and India have been ongoing for a long time through various bilateral mechanisms. However, the challenge of resolving differences over water use and benefit sharing remains to move forward with important projects like Pancheshwar. In such a situation, former diplomats suggest that the Prime Minister's visit should be used as an opportunity to seek concrete progress in water resources cooperation. Parvati Bhandari, Nepal News Bank
